headline: LNG Costs, Moa Point Sewage Disaster and Workplace Safety Bill Dominate New Zealand Parliament
summary: Parliament’s sitting was dominated by questions about household energy costs, Wellington’s Moa Point wastewater failure, and public-service safety, alongside a sharp election-year clash over the Government’s record. Ministers defended an LNG import terminal and changes to workplace safety rules, while opposition MPs challenged their costs and consequences. The House backed the Government’s 2026 programme and advanced a workplace safety bill, but adjourned before completing the final reading of legislation broadening Anzac Day commemorations.

topicSummaries.topic: LNG Terminal’s Cost and Effect on Power Bills Remain Unresolved
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed terminal could affect electricity prices and household bills, but its final cost and the rules governing its use have not yet been disclosed.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Megan Woods and Green MP Scott Willis pressed Energy Minister Simon Watts on the proposed liquefied natural gas import terminal, including whether its costs would be passed on to consumers and whether it would be limited to dry-year electricity backup. Watts said procurement negotiations were ongoing, so the total cost was not yet available, and described LNG as insurance for periods when hydro, wind and solar generation are insufficient. He said officials had considered alternatives and that the Electricity Authority’s powers would be strengthened to protect consumers. Opposition MPs questioned whether the project could instead increase costs or whether investment in renewables and energy efficiency would be preferable; no specific mechanism to restrict LNG use to dry years was given.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Megan Woods (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: What specific mechanisms will be put in place to make sure liquefied natural gas (LNG) is only used in dry years and not as routine baseload supply, which would push up energy costs for New Zealand households and businesses?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The reason why the Government is developing an LNG facility is to provide back-up fuel for electricity generation in a dry year. It is an insurance product for the electricity system.

topicSummaries.topic: Moa Point Wastewater Failure Prompts Blame and Calls for Investigation
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The failure has raised concerns about sewage entering Wellington’s coastal environment and whether water infrastructure and its operators are adequately funded and accountable.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Tamatha Paul questioned Local Government Minister Simon Watts about the Moa Point wastewater failure, water discharge standards and whether the Government’s decision to replace the Three Waters programme had contributed to underinvestment. Watts said it was too early to assign responsibility and pointed to longstanding underinvestment in water assets by local government. He said the Government, the Prime Minister and Wellington Mayor Andrew Little were considering an intervention and review, with the plant’s contracting arrangements among matters for consideration. Paul also questioned the role of operator Veolia; the Minister said councils were responsible for contracts and rejected her characterisation of the incident as privatising profits and socialising risks.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tamatha Paul (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he plan on holding Veolia to account for their environmental destruction, and, if not, is it his view that Veolia are not responsible for the ecological disaster happening on the south coast?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simon Watts (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We are looking and considering the intervention and the review process which we will undertake to get answers to those questions, and I have offered Mayor Little all of the support that I can provide from local government to make that happen. It is too early to signal or assign blame to anyone, but it would be fair to say years of under-investment will be, no doubt, part of the consideration by that group.

topicSummaries.topic: Firefighter Equipment Failures Put Front-Line Safety Under Scrutiny
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Reliable fire appliances and adequate staffing affect how quickly crews can respond and the risks they face at emergencies.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Lemauga Lydia Sosene challenged Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden over reported breakdowns of aerial appliances, including failures during a recent fire at Taupō-nui-a-Tia College, and questioned proposed annual savings of more than $50 million from Fire and Emergency New Zealand. Van Velden said the agency maintained a fleet of about 1,300 trucks, was replacing older vehicles and had five new aerial appliances due this year at a cost of $12.5 million. She said operational failures did not mean crews would not respond, citing backup resources, and maintained that the savings target concerned back-office efficiency rather than front-line trucks or maintenance. Labour also raised a Police Association report that nearly 60 percent of officers had considered leaving because of pay and staffing concerns; the Government pointed to additional funding and increased officer numbers.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lemauga Lydia Sosene (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why, in the face of repeated equipment failures, which are forcing firefighters to put their lives on the line—including climbing up the sides of burning buildings due to aerial failures—is she cutting more than $50 million a year from the Fire and Emergency New Zealand budget?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: One of the things I want to make abundantly clear is that there are no cuts to front-line trucks and maintenance, like the member seems to be alluding to.

topicSummaries.topic: Workplace Safety Bill Passes First Reading Amid Warnings of Weaker Protections
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed changes could alter employers’ obligations and the safety protections workers receive, particularly in businesses with fewer than 20 employees.
topicSummaries.content: Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden said the Health and Safety at Work Amendment Bill would focus obligations on serious or “critical” risks, make approved codes of practice a safe harbour for compliance, and reduce paperwork and costs for small businesses. Businesses with fewer than 20 workers for at least nine months of the year would have core duties focused on critical risks, while larger businesses would still have to manage all risks. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed the bill, arguing that the definition of critical risk could be unclear, that smaller businesses would have reduced duties, and that musculoskeletal and psychological harm might receive insufficient attention. National and New Zealand First supported sending the bill to the Education and Workforce Committee. It passed its first reading 68 votes to 53 and is due back from the committee by 13 June 2026.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: It focuses on what matters most: managing critical risks. It reduces unnecessary compliance costs, particularly for small business, and it provides greater clarity and confidence for workers and businesses.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Jan Tinetti (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill, despite its intentions—and I do acknowledge the intentions of it—risks making New Zealand’s health and safety at work area and landscape worse.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Wins Confidence Vote as Parties Clash Over Cost of Living
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The debate highlighted competing claims about household pressures, public services and the economy ahead of the 2026 election.
topicSummaries.content: The House rejected Labour leader Chris Hipkins’ motion of no confidence in the Government by 68 votes to 53, then passed a motion expressing confidence in the Government and endorsing its 2026 programme by the same margin. Labour MPs argued that groceries, power, insurance and healthcare remained unaffordable for many, and criticised the Government over housing and public-service funding. National ministers defended their economic approach, saying they were addressing the previous administration’s fiscal record and improving health, education and law and order. Labour also attacked the proposed LNG project’s consumer levy as an added cost, while ministers said the project would ultimately lower energy prices. The competing economic claims remained unresolved in the debate.

keyExchanges.speaker: Dr Tracey McLellan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The actual basics—the real basics that people care about—just get more expensive: groceries, power bills, insurance, healthcare.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We have a big job in this Government to fix—fixing the basics. That is a tough job. We are making the tough decisions that the last Government wouldn’t make.

topicSummaries.topic: Roads Programme Faces $30 Billion Funding Gap
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: How major roads are funded could affect transport charges and the money available for other infrastructure and public services.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Tangi Utikere questioned Transport Minister Chris Bishop about officials’ advice that the first wave of Roads of National Significance faced a $30 billion funding gap over the next decade. Bishop acknowledged substantial funding challenges and said the Government was working on a mix of options, including tolls, other charges and fuel taxes. He ruled out both a 50-cent-a-litre fuel tax increase and borrowing $40 billion as unrealistic, but did not announce a final funding plan. Bishop said the Government remained committed to a long-term transport pipeline that included roads and public transport projects, and announced that Transmission Gully would have its speed limit raised to 110 kilometres per hour.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tangi Utikere (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he accept that his own officials’ modelling shows that there are only two viable ways to fund this programme: either significantly higher transport taxes, or around $40 billion in additional debt; if so, which of those will he choose?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: However, within those broad strawmen that make the point, there are a range of different options, including tolls and other forms of charges and fuel tax.

topicSummaries.topic: Online Casino Bill Faces Questions Over Age Limits and Gambling Harm
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed licensing system would regulate online casinos and set rules for access, advertising and contributions to gambling-harm prevention.
topicSummaries.content: Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara questioned Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden about the Online Casino Gambling Bill, including its proposed 15 licences, access for 18- and 19-year-olds, and the potential effect on vulnerable communities. Van Velden said the current online market was unregulated and that the bill would prohibit under-18s from using licensed services or being targeted by their advertising. She argued that licensed operators would face harm-minimisation standards and contribute to the problem gambling levy. Kaipara cited a Salvation Army report estimating New Zealanders lost $2.79 billion to gambling in the previous year; the licensing auction has not yet taken place, and the bill had not become law.

keyExchanges.speaker: Oriini Kaipara (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: Why will this bill enable rangatahi aged 18 to access online casino gambling when existing laws prohibit anyone under 20 from walking through the door of a casino anywhere in the country?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Because currently, anybody of any age can gamble online. The law, when this bill is passed, will prohibit licensed casinos online from advertising to people under the age of 18 or allowing anybody under the age of 18 to use their products online.

topicSummaries.topic: Anzac Day Bill Debate Adjourned Before Final Vote
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed law would broaden official Anzac Day commemorations to include more New Zealanders who served in conflicts and related roles.
topicSummaries.content: The House continued the third-reading debate on the Anzac Day Amendment Bill, which would remove the existing limit to specified conflicts and include service in later conflicts, peacekeeping, military training and some non-military roles connected with service. Speakers from across parties expressed support for the broader commemoration, while discussing the experiences of veterans, families and communities. The debate was interrupted before the final vote so the remaining members could speak; it was set down to resume at the next sitting on 17 February. The bill therefore had not completed its third reading when the House adjourned.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Chris Penk (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Therefore, when enacted, the Anzac Day Act, as we will have amended it, will be more inclusive in terms of the type of service given.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Boyack (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: What the amendment bill does is it provides a broader and more inclusive Anzac Day recognition and commemoration by removing the limitation on specified named conflicts in which those who have served are recognised and commemorated.

topicSummaries.topic: Investment Boost Survey Reports Early Uptake Among Firms
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Business investment can affect productivity, employment and wages, while the policy’s longer-term economic effects remain projections.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis cited initial Inland Revenue survey results from more than 800 firms on Investment Boost, a tax measure introduced in Budget 2025 to encourage capital investment. She said 40 percent of firms aware of the scheme that had invested reported that it had increased their investment, including 11 percent who reported a significant increase. Willis also said 49 percent of firms planning to invest over the next five years expected the policy to influence their plans positively. She pointed to modelling that projects higher GDP, wages and capital stock over 20 years; the results presented were early survey findings rather than a final evaluation of the policy’s long-term effects.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The survey shows that of those who knew of the scheme, 40 percent of firms that invested said that Investment Boost had already increased their investment.

keyExchanges.speaker: Nancy Lu (National)
keyExchanges.quote: How important is policy certainty to long-term growth?

conclusion: The Government retained the House’s confidence and advanced its workplace safety bill, while disputes over household costs, infrastructure funding and public-service risks continued and the Anzac Day bill awaited a final vote.
